# Personalization as a retail sales lever
## Prepared for Michael Lee, Sales Team Lead

### Executive summary
Personalization can help retailers sell by reducing product-search friction, recommending useful complements, prompting timely replenishment, and connecting a consistent experience across stores, web, app, and delivery. Grocery and retail studies indicate that shoppers expect relevant digital experiences, but the evidence reviewed here does not establish a reliable sales uplift for Lee’s Market.

Lee’s internal records show meaningful loyalty and channel activity, plus a reported recommendation-engagement/AOV result. These are useful starting points, not proof that personalization caused sales growth. The recommendation is to verify the metric definitions and run a small, controlled pilot with incremental gross margin as the primary success measure.

### How personalization can drive sales
- **Help customers find relevant products.** Use a shopper’s own purchase and browsing history, plus preferences they explicitly choose, to rank products, recipes, and offers. Mastercard’s 2024 online-grocery article reports that 76.5% of grocery customers expect a tailored digital experience and are frustrated when it is missing. The supplied search evidence does not include the article’s sample or method, so treat this as a directional expectation signal rather than a Lee’s forecast. [1]
- **Build baskets with useful complements.** Test meal and occasion bundles—such as hot-pot or barbecue ingredients—when a customer has shown interest in those products. Use real-time store availability for fresh produce, meat, seafood, bakery, and prepared foods. Measure added margin after discounts rather than gross basket value alone.
- **Encourage repeat visits.** Test replenishment prompts for products a customer regularly buys and loyalty offers for relevant categories. Use customer-level holdouts to learn whether a reminder or offer creates an additional purchase or only discounts a planned one.
- **Make the experience coherent across channels.** Carry customer-selected preferences and eligible offers between website, app, checkout, and delivery. For Lee’s, translate the digital-experience expectation into a pilot that covers browse, cart, checkout, and post-purchase, with offers consistent across store and delivery. [1][4]

The broader evidence is promising but not causal. Deloitte reports that 80% of surveyed consumers preferred brands offering personalized experiences and reported spending 50% more with those brands. It also reports that 92% of retailers believed they personalized effectively, while 48% of consumers agreed. The page does not provide detailed study methods in the supplied material, and the spending association does not show that personalization caused the difference. [2] A dunnhumby article reports that 71% of surveyed Singaporean shoppers said they were more likely to buy from brands that treated them as individuals; that is a signal from a different market, not a forecast for Lee’s U.S. and Canadian stores. [3] Supermarket News describes Tesco’s Clubcard Challenges for more than 10 million UK customers, but gives no quantified sales lift in the supplied article text. [4]

### What Lee’s internal evidence says
- **Loyalty reach and spend have grown.** Lee’s loyalty workbook reports 720,000 members and average spend per member of 20 in Q2 2022, versus 1,200,000 members and 25 in Q3 2024. Total member spend rose from 14,400,000 to 30,000,000 over those endpoints. This is approximately 66.7% member growth, 25% spend-per-member growth, and 108.3% total member-spend growth. Currency is not specified, and the workbook does not attribute growth to personalization. [6]
- **Online channels show separate historical growth comparisons.** The online-sales workbook lists website sales of 150,000 for Q2 2024 versus Q2 2023 with a growth value of 12; mobile app sales of 100,000 for Q4 2023 versus Q4 2022 with a growth value of 10; and delivery sales of 80,000 for Q3 2023 versus Q3 2022 with a growth value of 6. The sheet labels these as growth rates, but the raw cells omit percent signs and the currency is unspecified. Validate the units before using them as a baseline. These are distinct channel-period comparisons, not one company-wide growth rate or evidence of personalization impact. [7]
- **Personalization performance is reported but unverified.** An indexed strategy document, titled “Personalized Retail Strategies for Growth,” says 45% of online customers engaged with personalized recommendations and reports a 25% AOV increase associated with that engagement. It also mentions a recommendation pilot for loyalty members. It provides no reporting period, engagement denominator, sample size, AOV baseline, control group, calculation, attribution method, or pilot result; the original author and file provenance are not established. Validate the figures against source systems before treating them as Lee’s results or targets. [8]
- **Customer identification needs a current baseline.** Samantha Kim reported that about 85% of transactions were linked to loyalty accounts and that the rate had improved from the previous quarter. Her message says “as of Q2 2024,” but its timestamp is 1 July 2023 at 21:21 UTC. Confirm the period and denominator. Transaction linkage is not the same as having a complete profile or marketing consent. [5]
- **Customer feedback is limited.** An internal message says survey results were uploaded, but the indexed material has no scores, response counts, or methodology. Separate positive comments about Asian snack variety/quality and the online platform are anecdotes, not representative satisfaction measures. [9]

### Recommended action plan
**Days 1–30: verify the data and establish baselines.** Reconcile the 85% transaction-link figure with POS, loyalty, e-commerce, and delivery records. Confirm the period, denominator, and channel/store variation. Validate the 45% engagement and 25% AOV figures, including the eligible population, exposure window, and calculation. Confirm the units and currency in the online-sales workbook. Establish current baselines for conversion, AOV, gross margin, repeat purchase, offer redemption, stock availability, and opt-outs.

**Days 31–60: run a narrow, customer-led pilot.** Select stores and online cohorts with enough eligible volume. Test (1) recommendations or meal bundles based on a customer’s own recent purchases and selected preferences, and (2) a relevant loyalty offer for a complement or replenishment occasion. Include website/app and store or delivery touchpoints where identity matching is reliable. Keep recommendations tied to available assortment and inventory, especially for fresh categories.

Let shoppers choose language and any dietary or product preferences they want used. Base segments on observed shopping behaviour or explicit choices, not inferred ethnicity, health status, or other sensitive traits. Set contact-frequency limits and make preference changes and opt-out simple.

**Days 61–90: measure incremental results.** Randomly assign eligible customers to personalized treatment or the usual experience. Keep timing and offer value comparable. Make incremental gross margin per eligible customer the primary measure; also track conversion, AOV, items per basket, category attachment, redemption, repeat visits, discount cost, stockouts/substitutions, and opt-outs or complaints. Add a direct customer-satisfaction measure because the current survey evidence lacks results. Scale only experiences that outperform the holdout after discount and operating costs.

### Management decision
Approve a 90-day baseline audit and controlled pilot. Release broader campaign spend only after the metric definitions, consent rules, control group, and margin measure are agreed. Lee’s loyalty and online channels offer a practical base for testing, but neither public survey findings nor the internal records justify promising a fixed sales lift.

### Sources
[1] Mastercard, “Personalization’s influence and necessity across the online grocery journey” (2024). The search result reports the 76.5% expectation/frustration figure; study details were not available in the supplied evidence. https://www.mastercard.com/global/en/news-and-trends/Insights/2024/personalizations-influence-and-necessity-across-the-online-grocery-journey.html
[2] Deloitte, “Unlocking Customer Growth: Driving High Value Actions Through Personalization and Retail Media.” Publication date is not stated in the supplied page; it reports 2024 survey figures. https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/programs/chief-marketing-officer/articles/personalization-strategy-in-retail-media.html
[3] Mark Burton, Richard Dawson, and Julie Jeancolas, dunnhumby, “Exploring the evolution of personalisation in grocery retail: Part One,” 14 June 2022. https://www.dunnhumby.com/articles/exploring-the-evolution-of-personalisation-in-grocery-retail/
[4] Jeff Baskin, Supermarket News, “The intersection between loyalty, personalization, retail media and AI,” 2 June 2025. https://www.supermarketnews.com/grocery-technology/the-intersection-between-loyalty-personalization-retail-media-and-ai
[5] MatterMost-Sales Strategy-Sales Team-Samantha Kim; post timestamp 1 July 2023 21:21 UTC, message text says “as of Q2 2024.”
[6] Lees_Market_Loyalty_Program_Performance_Metrics.xlsx, sheet “Loyalty Program Performance”; currency unspecified.
[7] Lees_Market_Online_Sales_Growth_Report.xlsx, sheet “Online Sales Growth”; raw growth-rate cells omit percent signs and currency is unspecified.
[8] tmpmvopvsxq.docx, indexed title “Personalized Retail Strategies for Growth”; original author, location, and version provenance unavailable.
[9] MatterMost-Customer Data-Customer Insights-Samantha Kim (survey-results upload message, June 2023); MatterMost-Sales Strategy-Sales Team-Emily Chen (Asian snack comment, May 2023); MatterMost-Sales Strategy-Sales Team-David Kim (online-platform feedback, October 2023).

report_insights.claim: Retail personalization can support discovery, basket building, repeat purchase, and cross-channel convenience, but public survey figures are not causal estimates of Lee’s sales lift.
Lee’s loyalty-member count, member spend, and total member spend increased across Q2 2022 to Q3 2024, but the workbook does not connect those historical gains to personalization.

The online-sales workbook lists distinct website, app, and delivery growth comparisons; raw rate cells omit percent signs and currency is unspecified, so validate definitions before using them as baselines.
An indexed strategy document reports 45% online recommendation engagement and a 25% AOV increase, but provides no methods, comparison group, period, or verified original-file provenance.
